title: UAE Healthcare providers urged to strengthen early referral pathways for pulmonary fibrosis
summary: Pulmonary fibrosis refers to scarring of lung tissue and can occur in several interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), a group of conditions affecting the tissue surrounding the air sacs.
thbAction: Pitch THB's diagnostics CRM to help labs manage doctor outreach, collection-center expansion, and B2B referral relationships while improving conversion and retention.
contentHtml:
By Prof. Dr. Syed Arshad Husain, Consultant Pulmonologist, Al Zahra Hospital Dubai

UAE – Healthcare providers in the UAE are being encouraged to strengthen referral pathways for suspected pulmonary fibrosis in 2027 by improving clinical documentation, specialist follow-up and monitoring of diagnostic delays.

Prof. Dr. Syed Arshad Husain, Consultant Pulmonologist at Al Zahra Hospital Dubai, said persistent dry cough and worsening breathlessness during physical activity should prompt further assessment for pulmonary fibrosis.

He emphasised that referrals should clearly document the symptoms, available imaging, and lung function results, as well as identify the healthcare professional responsible for ensuring the patient reaches a specialist.

The recommendation follows a pulmonary fibrosis awareness campaign covered by Healthcare Middle East & Africa in October 2026, which sought to improve recognition of the condition among patients and healthcare professionals across the UAE.

For 2027, measuring the time between initial suspicion and a completed specialist consultation could help healthcare providers identify gaps in the diagnostic pathway.

Recognising pulmonary fibrosis in primary care

Pulmonary fibrosis occurs when lung tissue becomes scarred, making it harder for the lungs to transfer oxygen into the bloodstream.

It can develop in several interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), a group of conditions that affect the tissue surrounding the air sacs.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a specific form in which clinicians cannot identify an underlying cause after investigation.

Distinguishing between suspected fibrotic lung disease and confirmed IPF is important because primary care clinicians can identify warning signs, while respiratory specialists determine the underlying condition and appropriate treatment.

The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) identifies persistent breathlessness during exertion, persistent cough and crackles heard in both lungs during inhalation as features that should raise suspicion of IPF, particularly among older adults.

Importantly, spirometry results may remain normal in some patients.

Therefore, a normal result should not end further investigation when symptoms persist or exercise tolerance continues to decline.

Clinical findings and existing imaging can help respiratory specialists determine the need for additional investigations and prioritise appointments.

Imaging reports can improve referral decisions

Evidence published in Respiratory Research highlights the importance of communicating imaging findings during referrals.

The study found that patients whose chest CT reports mentioned interstitial lung disease were more likely to receive a pulmonology referral within six months of the scan.

The association had a rate ratio of 2.17, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.03 to 4.56.

Although the observational findings do not establish that changing the wording of radiology reports alone accelerates referrals, they highlight an opportunity to improve communication between radiologists, primary care clinicians and respiratory specialists.

Referring clinicians should therefore include relevant CT findings in their referral letters and ensure specialists can access the original scan images.

A standardised referral template could further improve the quality and consistency of information shared between healthcare facilities.

It should capture the duration of symptoms, changes in walking ability, clinical findings such as crackles and available imaging and lung function results.

Where available, clinicians should also document smoking history, occupational and household exposures, relevant medications and any known autoimmune conditions.

They should identify outstanding investigations so that respiratory teams can assess the referral using the information already available.

Based on these findings, specialists can determine whether the patient needs a dedicated high-resolution CT scan, additional lung function testing or assessment by a thoracic radiologist and other relevant specialists.

Diagnostic delays highlight gaps in patient pathways

The time required to diagnose pulmonary fibrosis remains a concern for healthcare systems.

A Danish study involving 264 people newly diagnosed with IPF found that the median interval between the first symptoms and diagnosis was two years.

Half of the participants experienced delays ranging from 0.9 to five years.

The researchers also found an association between longer diagnostic delays and a higher risk of disease progression or death, with a hazard ratio of 1.70 and a 95% confidence interval of 1.18 to 2.46.

These findings reflect the experience of patients in Denmark and should not be interpreted as evidence of similar waiting times in the UAE.

However, they highlight the importance of monitoring diagnostic pathways and identifying avoidable delays between primary care assessment, specialist referral and diagnosis.

For UAE healthcare providers, this creates an opportunity to strengthen coordination between primary care clinics, diagnostic imaging departments and specialist respiratory services.

Better referral management could also help hospitals identify capacity constraints and allocate specialist appointments according to clinical urgency.

Measuring referral performance in 2027

A clinic network could establish baseline referral performance during the first quarter of 2027 by tracking two intervals.

The first would measure the time from the initial documented suspicion of fibrotic lung disease to submission of the referral.

The second would measure the time from referral submission to the patient’s first completed respiratory consultation.

Healthcare providers could compare median waiting times across subsequent quarters to assess changes in referral performance.

They should also report referral volumes and the proportion of patients still awaiting appointments to ensure that incomplete cases remain visible in performance assessments.

Assigning responsibility for tracking individual referrals would provide another layer of accountability.

A designated clinician or care coordinator should confirm that the specialist service has received the referral, establish whether the patient attended the appointment and arrange follow-up when a consultation does not take place.

After the specialist assessment, the referring team and patient should receive clear information about the findings and the next steps in care.

This would help maintain continuity between primary and specialist services while reducing the risk of patients being lost during the referral process.

For healthcare providers and hospital networks, these measures offer a practical way to assess referral efficiency, improve coordination between departments and identify weaknesses in the management of suspected pulmonary fibrosis.
